subject: Archaeology
title: The Deir el-Medina Workers
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: The Deir el-Medina Workers.

hook.text: Ancient Egypt had a workers' strike 3,000 years before modern labor movements. The pharaoh did not pay them.

buildup.text: Deir el-Medina was a village of tomb builders who lived near the Valley of the Kings for generations.

discovery.text: Workers kept diaries on limestone flakes. They recorded attendance, pay disputes, and even love letters.

twist.text: In 1155 BCE, workers marched out when their grain rations stopped. It is history's first recorded labor strike.

climax.text: The village was so well preserved that we know more about these workers' lives than about most pharaohs.

punchline.text: Ordinary workers left better records than the kings they served.

quiz.question: What makes the Deir el-Medina strike historically significant?
options: It led to the overthrow of the pharaoh
It is the first recorded labor strike in history
Workers demanded the right to elect their own leaders

details.summary: Deir el-Medina was a village housing workers who built the royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings. Thousands of preserved ostraca — inscribed pottery fragments — reveal their daily lives, including work schedules, pay disputes, and the first recorded labor strike.
details.whyItMatters: Deir el-Medina provides the most detailed picture of ordinary Egyptian life anywhere. These workers' records humanize ancient Egypt beyond pharaohs and temples, revealing a literate working class with legal rights.
takeaways: Workers who built royal tombs lived in this planned village
Ostraca reveal daily life, pay records, and legal disputes
The village records the world's first known labor strike

faq.question: What was the first recorded labor strike about?
faq.answer: Around 1170 BCE under Ramesses III, workers stopped building when their grain rations were not delivered. They marched to temples demanding payment, chanting that they were hungry. Officials eventually provided the overdue rations, ending the protest.

faq.question: What do ostraca from Deir el-Medina reveal?
faq.answer: These inscribed pottery fragments contain everything from work attendance records and supply lists to love poems, medical prescriptions, and legal complaints. They reveal a literate community with complex social lives, property rights, and divorce proceedings.
